title: Diffusion Model's Generalization Can Be Characterized by Inductive Biases toward a Data-Dependent Ridge Manifold
claim: Generated samples evolve in distinct phases, first reaching a data-dependent ridge, then aligning to it, then sliding along it.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right, phase-labeled; zoom-in insets with arrows in last two
description: Four side-by-side 2-D scatter plots, labeled (a) early phase, (b) reach, (c) align and (d) slide. They show the progression of generated samples in a toy semi-circular dataset. Red crosses mark nine true data centers on a semi-circle, and blue dots are generated samples. A green curve is the log-density ridge, drawn over an orange density heatmap. In (a) the samples form a diffuse Gaussian blob near the origin, away from the ridge. In (b) they spread along the arc, near the ridge. In (c) they concentrate tightly on the ridge. Two zoom-in boxes show local detail. In (d) the samples slide toward the nearby data centers. The zoom insets show red arrows for sliding direction and green arrows for continued alignment. A legend in each panel's top right names the symbols.
caption: Reach-align-slide on semi-circular dataset: 9 unevenly spaced data points (red crosses) lie on a semi-circle of radius 4 centered at the origin. Generated samples (blue dots) evolve relative to the log-density ridge (green curve), exhibiting the reach–align–slide pattern. The zoom-in boxes in (c),(d) show region-dependent sliding: red arrows denote sliding directions and green arrows denote directions of continuation of alignment phase, with arrow lengths indicating intensity.
abstract: We study a data-dependent notion of diffusion-model generalization: when a model does not memorize the training set, where do its generated samples go relative to the geometry induced by the data? To answer this, we introduce a time-dependent family of log-density ridge manifolds constructed from the smoothed empirical distribution, and use it to characterize reverse-time inference. Our main result shows that generated samples evolve by a reach-align-slide mechanism: they first enter a neighborhood of the ridge, then their distance to the ridge is controlled by the normal component of training error, and finally their motion along the ridge is controlled by the tangential component. We further connect this geometric picture to training dynamics through directional decompositions of the learned error, and make this link explicit for random feature models, where architectural bias and optimization error can be separated quantitatively. Experiments on synthetic multimodal data and MNIST latent diffusion support the predicted geometric behavior in both low and high dimensions.
